comp-withdrawal-comparison-current-li-2: Rewards are not paid out automatically — claim them explicitly with the validator tooling, or delegate reward management to your operator setup
comp-withdrawal-comparison-current-p: Enter your validator address below to view its details on Quantaureum Explorer. Your staked balance and reward address are listed under the validator details.

comp-withdrawal-comparison-new-li-2: This is not required at bond time, but setting it early avoids moving rewards manually later

page-staking-image-alt: Illustration of a validator node securing the network.
page-staking-benefits-1-description: Rewards are given for actions that help the network reach consensus. You earn rewards for running software that proposes blocks and checks the work of other validators — that is what keeps the chain running securely.
page-staking-benefits-2-description: The network gets stronger against attacks as more QAU is staked. To become a threat, an attacker would need to control the majority of all staked QAU. By staking, you add to the pool of honest validators an attacker must overcome.
page-staking-benefits-3-description: Validators do not perform energy-intensive proof-of-work computations. Staking nodes run on modest hardware using very little energy, securing the network at a tiny fraction of the cost of mining.
page-staking-hero-subtitle: Run a validator with a minimum bond of 32 QAU and earn protocol rewards for keeping the chain final.
page-staking-section-what-p1: Staking is the act of bonding QAU to activate a validator — a participant in Quantaureum's QPOS consensus. Validators propose blocks and check each other's work; a validator requires a minimum bond of 32 QAU and can hold up to 6,600,000 QAU. Delegators can join with as little as 1 QAU by bonding to an existing validator, which charges a commission on rewards.
page-staking-section-what-p2: Staking is two things at once. For Quantaureum, it is the security mechanism at the heart of QPOS: the QAU validators put at stake is what makes their votes on the state of the chain trustworthy, because an attacker would need to control the majority of all staked QAU to threaten the network. For you, staking is a way to earn QAU rewards for participating honestly in that process.
page-staking-section-what-p3: Honesty is enforced with penalties. Validators that miss their slots lose the rewards for those slots, while provable misbehavior — such as signing two conflicting blocks — results in slashing: 5% of the validator's bond is destroyed and the validator is permanently removed from the active set.
page-staking-section-how-to-p1: It depends on how much you are willing to bond, and how directly you want to operate. You need at least 32 QAU to run your own validator, or as little as 1 QAU to delegate to one.
page-staking-section-how-to-p2: The options below are ordered from most protocol-native to most abstracted. Operating your own validator is the baseline: you hold your own keys and the protocol pays you directly. Each option after it solves a real access problem — less QAU, no hardware, or more convenience — in exchange for trusting an operator or contract with your funds.
page-staking-hierarchy-solo-p1: Running your own validator is the gold standard for staking on Quantaureum. Nothing stands between you and the protocol: you hold your own Dilithium signing keys, and the protocol pays full rewards directly to your reward address. It also strengthens the decentralization of the validator set.
page-staking-hierarchy-solo-p2: Self-operating validators should have at least 32 QAU plus a buffer for transaction fees, and a dedicated machine connected to the internet around the clock. Some technical know-how is helpful — the node software and validator tooling are open source.
page-staking-hierarchy-solo-p3: Rewards accrue every block but are not paid out automatically: claim them explicitly with the validator tooling. Before bonding on mainnet, rehearse the full flow on testnet. Run a node to get started.
page-staking-hierarchy-saas-p1: If you do not want to deal with hardware, delegation lets a validator operator run the node while you keep ownership of the bonded QAU. The operator charges a commission (between 1% and 100%) on the rewards your stake earns.
page-staking-hierarchy-saas-p2: Delegating requires a minimum of 1 QAU. You keep custody of your funds; the operator never holds them. What you delegate is trust in their operation: a badly run node simply earns less, but a compromised operator can affect your rewards.
page-staking-hierarchy-saas-p3: Choose operators carefully — check their uptime, commission, and community reputation before bonding. Delegation markets on Quantaureum are still young; verify any operator's identity independently before transferring stake.
page-staking-hierarchy-pools-p1: Delegating through the protocol issues STQAU, a QRC-20 receipt token that represents your staked QAU plus accrued rewards.
page-staking-hierarchy-pools-p2: Because STQAU is a standard QRC-20 token, it can be held in any Quantaureum wallet, moved, or used on-chain while your original stake keeps validating.
page-staking-hierarchy-pools-p3: Third-party liquid staking services are not yet established on Quantaureum. Anything presenting itself as such should be verified independently before you send funds.
page-staking-hierarchy-pools-p4: STQAU is issued by the protocol itself; it is not a claim on any third party. The underlying validator still controls validation, and rewards follow the operator's commission.
page-staking-hierarchy-cex-p1: Some centralized exchanges may offer staking services for QAU. They can be a fallback to earn some yield with minimal effort, if you are not yet comfortable holding QAU in your own wallet.
page-staking-hierarchy-cex-p2: The trade-off is that exchanges consolidate large pools of QAU. This creates a large centralized target and point of failure, which is dangerous for the network and its users. No exchange listing implies any endorsement — verify everything independently.
page-staking-hierarchy-cex-p3: If you don't feel comfortable holding your own <link1>keys</link1>, that's okay. These options are here for you. In the meantime, consider checking out our <link2>wallets page</link2> to learn how to take true ownership over your funds.
page-staking-hierarchy-subtext: As you may have noticed, there are several ways to participate in Quantaureum staking. These paths target different users and vary in risks, rewards, and trust assumptions. We describe what the protocol itself supports; always do your own research before sending QAU anywhere.
page-staking-comparison-solo-saas: Delegating keeps your bonded QAU yours, but hands day-to-day operation to an operator who takes a commission on your rewards. Self-operating gives you the full rewards and full responsibility: hardware, uptime, and key security. If you can operate a node, self-operating is the stronger option for you and for the network.
page-staking-comparison-solo-pools: Self-operating is more involved than delegating, but offers full access to protocol rewards and full control over your validator. Delegating has a much lower barrier to entry — from 1 QAU — and issues a tradeable STQAU receipt, at the cost of the operator's commission and trust in their operation.
page-staking-comparison-saas-solo: Both keep ownership of the bonded funds with you, but delegation requires trusting a third party's operation. If these trust assumptions concern you, the gold standard is running your own validator.
page-staking-comparison-saas-pools: Both let you participate without running hardware yourself. Delegation bonds your QAU to an operator; the STQAU receipt keeps your position visible and transferable on-chain.
page-staking-comparison-pools-solo: Delegating has a much lower barrier to entry than self-operating, but the operator charges a commission and runs the node on your behalf. Self-operating gives full sovereignty: you hold the keys, you claim the rewards, no middleman takes a cut.
page-staking-comparison-pools-saas: Both routes delegate the validation work. Direct delegation goes through the protocol's validator registry; third-party services would add their own layer on top — none are established yet.

page-staking-considerations-solo-5-descr: Validator keys are not entrusted to any other human at any time in the validator lifecycle. Any smart contracts involved are free of back doors, without reliance on privileged permissions for execution.
page-staking-considerations-solo-6-descr: Users do not require any special permission to operate a validator using the software or service
page-staking-considerations-solo-7-descr: The network currently ships one reference implementation; there is no client diversity choice to make
page-staking-considerations-solo-8-descr: User maintains custody of any validator credentials, including signing and reward keys
page-staking-considerations-solo-9-descr: Users can participate by delegating as little as 1 QAU to an existing validator

page-staking-considerations-saas-6-descr: Users do not require any special permission, account sign up or KYC to participate with the service
page-staking-considerations-saas-7-descr: Not applicable on Quantaureum today: the network runs a single reference client
page-staking-considerations-saas-8-descr: Not applicable on Quantaureum today: the validator set is the reference implementation

page-staking-launchpad-widget-p2: If you're comfortable with it, you can set up everything needed from the command line with the validator tooling alone.

page-staking-section-comparison-subtitle: There is no one-size-fits-all solution for staking. Here we compare the risks, rewards and requirements of the ways you can stake on Quantaureum.
page-staking-section-comparison-solo-rew: Maximum rewards, received in full directly from the protocol
Rewards for proposing blocks and for validating epochs; claimed explicitly via the validator tooling
A single validator may bond up to 6,600,000 QAU
page-staking-section-comparison-saas-rew: Protocol rewards minus the operator's commission (1%–100%)
No hardware or uptime responsibility on your side
page-staking-section-comparison-pools-re: Rewards accrue to your bonded position; the STQAU receipt token tracks your share
STQAU is a standard QRC-20 token you hold in your own wallet
STQAU can be transferred on-chain while the underlying stake keeps validating

Validator key compromise lets an attacker get you slashed — protect signing keys accordingly

Operation quality is out of your hands: missed slots reduce your rewards
page-staking-section-comparison-pools-ri: Delegation relies on the operator's honest operation; verify them independently

Basic command-line familiarity for setup, monitoring, and reward claiming

page-staking-glance-title: All staking approaches at a glance
page-staking-glance-description: The table below covers the paths the protocol supports today: self-operated validating, delegation to an existing validator, and custodial staking through centralized exchanges. Every step away from running your own validator adds an intermediary between you and the protocol.
page-staking-glance-home-keys: Yes. You hold the validator signing keys and the reward address.
page-staking-glance-home-hardware: Yes. You run your own node.
page-staking-glance-home-middleware: None. You interact directly with the protocol.
page-staking-glance-home-who-pays: The protocol pays you directly when you claim.
page-staking-glance-home-minimum-eth: 32 QAU (a single validator may bond up to 6,600,000 QAU).
page-staking-glance-bonded-keys: No. The operator holds the validator keys; you keep ownership of your delegated stake.
page-staking-glance-bonded-hardware: No. The operator runs the node.
page-staking-glance-bonded-who-pays: The protocol pays the validator; you receive your share minus commission.
page-staking-glance-delegated-keys: No. The operator controls validation; your stake stays yours.
page-staking-glance-delegated-hardware: No. The operator runs the node.
page-staking-glance-delegated-who-pays: The protocol pays your validator; the operator charges a commission on rewards.
page-staking-glance-pools-keys: No. The operator controls validation; you hold an STQAU receipt token.
page-staking-glance-pools-hardware: No. The operator runs the nodes.
page-staking-glance-pools-middleware: The operator's infrastructure and the STQAU receipt token.
page-staking-glance-pools-who-pays: The protocol, via the STQAU receipt's accrued rewards, minus commission.
page-staking-glance-cex-keys: No. The exchange has custody of your QAU.
page-staking-glance-cex-who-pays: The exchange, according to its terms.
page-staking-glance-restaking: Restaking is not part of QPOS. Bonded QAU secures the Quantaureum network only; there is no restaking mechanism in the protocol. More in the FAQ
page-staking-faq-1-answer: A validator is a participant in Quantaureum's QPOS consensus. Validators are represented by an address, a Dilithium public key, a bonded stake, and other properties. Validator software is what acts on behalf of the validator by holding and using its signing key.
page-staking-faq-2-question: Why do I need to have funds at stake?
page-staking-faq-2-answer: A validator has the ability to propose and verify blocks for the network. To prevent dishonest behavior, users must have their funds at stake. This allows the protocol to penalize malicious actors. Staking is a means to keep you honest, as your actions will have financial consequences.
page-staking-faq-3-answer-p1: There is no separate staking token in the protocol: the native currency is QAU, and staking does not change what it is.
page-staking-faq-3-answer-p2: Delegating stake issues STQAU, a QRC-20 receipt token that represents your bonded QAU plus accrued rewards. Learn more about liquid staking
page-staking-faq-4-answer-p1: Yes. Staking is live on Quantaureum mainnet (chain ID 1668) today.
page-staking-faq-4-answer-p2: This means that staking is currently live for users to bond QAU, run a validator, and start earning rewards.
page-staking-faq-4-answer-p3: Rehearse on testnet (chain ID 1669) first: generate validator keys, bond, and claim rewards end to end before committing mainnet funds.
page-staking-faq-5-question: When can I withdraw my staked QAU?
page-staking-faq-5-answer-p1: You can unbond at any time. Unbonding is subject to a cooldown before the stake becomes spendable again, so plan around that delay.
page-staking-faq-5-answer-p2: Rewards are not paid out automatically — claim them explicitly with the validator tooling to your configured reward address.
page-staking-faq-6-question: How much QAU do I need to stake?
page-staking-faq-6-answer-p1: At least 32 QAU to run your own validator, or from 1 QAU to delegate to one. A single validator may bond up to 6,600,000 QAU — the protocol caps how much a single validator can accumulate.
page-staking-faq-6-answer-p2: Validators charge a commission between 1% and 100% on the rewards your delegated stake earns; compare operators before bonding.
page-staking-faq-7-question: How long does it take to start staking?
page-staking-faq-7-answer-p1: After bonding, a new validator waits for the next activation window before joining the active set; on Quantaureum's 12-second blocks this is typically minutes, not weeks.
page-staking-faq-7-answer-p2: Unbonding similarly passes through a cooldown before funds are spendable. Delegating is quicker: your stake starts following the chosen validator once confirmed.
page-staking-faq-8-question: Is restaking the same as staking?
page-staking-faq-8-answer-p1: No. Restaking does not exist on Quantaureum. Bonded QAU secures the Quantaureum network only — the protocol has no mechanism to reuse stake to secure additional applications, and any service claiming otherwise is not part of the protocol.
